didactic

/dy-DAK-tik/ — rhymes with graphic · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Didactic describes something meant to teach a lesson, usually pressing its message in a preachy, lecturing way.

The fable is openly didactic, ending with its moral spelled out.

Example

A children's story explicitly teaches that honesty is the best policy — a didactic tale in which the characters learn the lesson and the narrator states it outright at the end.

This is clearly didactic because it's designed to teach a lesson in an obvious, instructive way. The word captures both the teaching intent and the somewhat heavy-handed style of stating the lesson outright.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

instructive: Instructive means giving useful knowledge or guidance — teaching that helps and then steps back. Didactic also means built to teach, but it adds a pushy tone: a didactic work presses its lesson on you, while an instructive one simply leaves you knowing more.

prescriptive: Prescriptive means laying down rules — telling people exactly what they must do and how. A didactic work teaches a lesson or a moral; a prescriptive one goes further and hands out requirements. Didactic pushes a message, while prescriptive issues orders.

moralistic: Moralistic means quick to judge and preach about right versus wrong. Didactic is wider: a didactic work pushes any lesson hard — grammar, history, safety — while a moralistic one specifically lectures its audience about good and bad behavior.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

entertaining: meant to amuse rather than instruct

lighthearted: playful and free of any serious lesson

Where it sits · how hard the lesson gets pushed

entertaining → engaging → didactic → preachy

entertaining vs. didactic: Entertaining sits at the opposite end of the scale from didactic: an entertaining story exists to delight its audience, while a didactic one exists to teach a lesson.

engaging vs. didactic: Engaging is more neutral than didactic: an engaging book simply holds your attention, while a didactic book holds your attention in order to instruct you.

preachy vs. didactic: Preachy is stronger than didactic: a didactic story teaches openly, but a preachy one pushes its moral so hard that readers feel lectured.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — didact: taught; to teach (from Greek didaskein, 'to teach')

Suffix — -ic: characteristic of (Greek)

Put it together: Didact ('taught,' from Greek didaskein, 'to teach') + -ic ('characteristic of') means 'characteristic of teaching' — didactic describes writing or speech designed to instruct, sometimes so insistently that it feels preachy.

Use the root in a new word: autodidact: Her favorite composer was an autodidact whose symphonies still pack concert halls — the didact in the word is the same Greek 'teach' root inside didactic.

Root Check

Word Choice

formal / literary

Didactic describes language or art that's clearly meant to teach a lesson, often in an obvious or heavy-handed way. Use it when analyzing fables, moral tales, and explicitly instructive writing. For entertainment or subtle learning, plain words like 'engaging' or 'thought-provoking' might fit better.
